place.zh: 石坳村 · 屋后柴垛 · 半夜

setup.zh: 它一整天没醒，尾根的断口渗着银色的血。半夜里，它睁开了一只眼睛。你问她：真的有仙人？
setup.en: It has not woken all day; silver blood seeps from the cuts at its tail. At midnight it opens one eye. You ask her: are there really immortals?

recap.zh: 银月醒了一回：仙人是真的，凡人能修。次夜她留下洗髓丹、《吐纳经》和一个「藏」字，钻进了木牌；那声谢谢，她没听见。
recap.en: Yinyue woke once: immortals are real, mortals can cultivate. The next night she left a Marrow-Washing Pill, *The Classic of Breathing* and one word — hide — and went into the token; the thank-you, she never heard.

zh: 柴垛上，一团凉冰冰的银毛。
断口渗出的血，是银的，像落了一层霜。
半夜，它睁开了一只眼睛。
en: On the woodpile, a cold curl of silver fur.
The blood from its cuts is silver, like a fall of frost.
At midnight, it opens one eye.

story.zh:
那天夜里，小满把「围脖」抱到了屋后的柴垛上。

屋里人多——其实只有三个，可一间屋住三个人，翻个身都要先跟旁边的人打声招呼，便显得多了。柴垛上没人，只有月亮。

它一整天都没醒。身子还是凉的，那一条尾巴垂着，尾根上那八道断口不知什么时候又渗出了血来，银色的，一滴一滴落在柴草上，像下了一层霜。小满拿袖子去擦，擦了又渗，渗了又擦，擦到后来，袖子上也结了一层霜。他便不擦了，把它捧在两只手里，搁在自己膝盖上，拿身子挡着风。

他守到半夜。半夜里，它睁开了一只眼睛。

头一句便是：「……吵死了。你喘气那么大声干什么。」

小满长长地松了一口气，松得太猛，差点哭出来，好歹憋住了。他道：「我喘气哪里大声了？」

「像拉风箱。」

「那是你没听过我爹打呼噜。」

「听过了。」它闭上那只眼睛，又睁开，「昨儿夜里，听过了。你们一家子，睡觉都不安生。」

他道：「你醒了就好。今儿马三来过了。」

「知道。」「你知道？」

「本王昏着，耳朵没昏。」它顿了一顿，「你那个吃饼的鬼，编得还凑合。还有那一把白胡子。」

小满道：「我娘说编得不好。说鬼不吃饼，下回说它吃香火。」

它沉默了一会儿，道：「……你娘说得对。」

小满把它往怀里挪了挪，道：「银月。你说你是从仙界掉下来的。」

「嗯。」

「仙界在哪？」

「上面。」

「比蒙山顶还高？」

「高多了。」

「那你掉下来的时候，疼不疼——」

银月一尾巴拍在他嘴上：「一个一个问。」

小满便一个一个地问。有一个问题，他从谷底憋到现在，这时候再也憋不住了：「你说你只剩『金丹』了。金丹……是金子做的丹吗？」银月不答。

「值钱吗？比鹿皮值钱吗？能换几斤肉？」

银月闭上了眼睛：「本王不想醒了。」

「还有『修为』。修为是什么？能吃吗？」

「不能。」

「那『修仙』呢？吴婆婆也说什么修仙。」小满皱着眉头，认认真真地琢磨，「是修房子的一种吗？修仙……仙人坏了，要人修？」

银月把脸埋进了自己的尾巴里，好半天没抬起来。过了良久，才闷闷地道：「好。好。本王从头说。你先说，你们凡人，知道仙人是什么？」小满想了一想，道：「吴婆婆讲过，蒙山顶上住过一个骑白鹤的老头，一顿饭吃一颗枣，活了八百岁。我爹说那是编的。」

「你爹说错了。」

小满的嘴，慢慢张大了。

银月道：「仙人，是真的。活八百岁的有，活八千岁的也有。骑鹤的，骑龙的，踩一片云就走的，都有。他们以前，也都是凡人——猎户，樵夫，种地的，读书的。后来学会了一样本事：把天地间的灵气，一点一点收进自己的身子里，炼成自己的东西。一年，十年，一百年。不老，不病，力能搬山，最后连天都关不住。」她顿了一顿，「这，就叫修仙。」

柴垛上很静。小满听见自己的心咚咚地跳，隔了好一会儿，才问：「骑龙的……是像吴婆婆讲的那个皇帝那样？」银月的耳朵，动了一下。「本王听见了。」她的声音很低，「……本王那时候，昏着。」「那是真的吗？」

银月没有答。她看着月亮，看了很久，久到小满以为她又睡着了，才道：「……本王不记得了。」她说的是「不记得」，不是「不知道」。小满当时没听出这两样有什么分别。

「那……我也能？」

「能。但很难。一百个凡人里，生得出灵根的，三五个。能修的人里，一百个，九十九个老死了事。」

「那剩下那一个呢？」

银月没有回答。她偏过头来，看着他，那双金色的眼睛慢慢合上了一半，道：「……你还有一肚子要问的。本王知道。可本王，答不动了。」

「那我问谁？」

「问他们。这世上有一群人，专门修仙，专门教人修仙。灵气是什么，丹田是什么，境界是什么——他们会告诉你。比本王，有耐心。」她停了一停，又补了一句，「……当然，没本王教得好。」

小满道：「那我上哪儿找他们去？」

「会有的……」她的声音越来越轻，轻到后来，便没有了。她睡着了，尾巴尖儿搭在他手腕上，搭在他娘打的那个方方正正的结上。
story.en:
That night Xiaoman carried the "scarf" out to the woodpile behind the house.

The house was crowded — really only three people, but with three people in one room you had to warn your neighbour before you turned over, so it felt crowded. On the woodpile there was nobody, only the moon.

It hadn't woken all day. Its body was still cold, its one tail hanging, and from the eight stumps at its root silver blood had begun to seep again, drop by drop onto the kindling, like a layer of frost. Xiaoman wiped it with his sleeve; wiped, and it seeped; seeped, and he wiped; till his sleeve too wore a layer of frost. Then he stopped wiping, and held it in both hands on his knee, shielding it from the wind with his body.

He kept watch till midnight. At midnight it opened one eye.

The first thing it said was: "…So noisy. Why do you breathe so loud."

Xiaoman let out a long breath — too hard; he nearly cried, and just managed to hold it in. "How am I breathing loud?"

"Like a bellows."

"You've never heard my dad snore."

"I have." It shut the eye and opened it again. "Last night — heard it. Your family can't even sleep quietly."

He said, "Good, you're awake. Ma San came today."

"I know." "You know?"

"This king was out cold; this king's ears were not." It paused. "That flatbread-eating ghost of yours — passable. And that white beard."

Xiaoman said, "My mum says it was bad. She says ghosts don't eat flatbread; next time say it eats incense."

It was silent a while, then said: "…Your mother's right."

Xiaoman shifted it further into his arms. "Yinyue. You said you fell from the Immortal Realm."

"Mm."

"Where's the Immortal Realm?"

"Up."

"Higher than the top of Mount Meng?"

"Much higher."

"Then when you fell, did it hurt —"

Yinyue slapped her tail across his mouth. "One question at a time."

So Xiaoman asked one at a time. One question he'd held in since the bottom of the valley, and now he couldn't hold it any more: "You said all you've got left is a 'golden core'. A golden core… is it a pill made of gold?" Yinyue didn't answer.

"Is it worth much? More than a deer hide? How many catties of meat would it get?"

Yinyue shut her eyes. "This king doesn't want to be awake."

"And 'cultivation'. What's cultivation? Can you eat it?"

"No."

"And 'cultivating immortality'? Granny Wu said something about that too." Xiaoman knitted his brows, pondering it very seriously. "Is it a kind of house repair? Cultivating immortals… the immortals are broken and need fixing?"

Yinyue buried her face in her own tail and didn't raise it for a good while. At last she said, muffled, "Fine. Fine. This king will start from the beginning. First you tell me — what do you mortals know of immortals?" Xiaoman thought, then said, "Granny Wu said once there was an old man who lived on top of Mount Meng and rode a white crane; he ate one jujube a meal and lived to eight hundred. My dad says it's made up."

"Your father's wrong."

Xiaoman's mouth slowly fell open.

Yinyue said: "Immortals are real. Some live eight hundred years, some eight thousand. Some ride cranes, some ride dragons, some step on a cloud and go. Once they were all mortals too — hunters, woodcutters, farmers, scholars. Then they learned one skill: to draw the spirit-qi of heaven and earth into their bodies, bit by bit, and make it their own. A year, ten years, a hundred. No ageing, no sickness, strong enough to move mountains, and in the end not even heaven can hold them." She paused. "That is called cultivating immortality."

It was very quiet on the woodpile. Xiaoman heard his heart thumping, and only after a good while asked, "The ones who ride dragons… like the emperor in Granny Wu's story?" Yinyue's ear twitched. "This king heard it." Her voice was very low. "…This king was unconscious at the time." "Is it true?"

Yinyue didn't answer. She looked at the moon a long time, so long Xiaoman thought she had fallen asleep again, before she said, "…This king doesn't remember." She said "doesn't remember", not "doesn't know". Xiaoman didn't hear the difference at the time.

"Then… could I?"

"You can. But it's hard. Out of a hundred mortals, three or five are born with a spirit root. Of those who can cultivate, ninety-nine in a hundred grow old and die and that's the end of it."

"And the one left?"

Yinyue didn't answer. She turned her head and looked at him, her golden eyes slowly half closing. "…You've a bellyful more to ask. This king knows. But this king can't answer any more."

"Then who do I ask?"

"Ask them. There's a sort of people in this world who do nothing but cultivate, and teach others to. What spirit-qi is, what the dantian is, what the realms are — they'll tell you. More patient than this king." She stopped, then added, "…Of course, not as good at teaching as this king."

Xiaoman said, "Then where do I find them?"

"There will be…" Her voice grew fainter and fainter, until it was gone. She was asleep, the tip of her tail resting on his wrist, on the neat square knot his mother had tied.

story.zh:
第二天，她没有醒。

小满隔一会儿便低头看一眼胸口，他娘问他胸口疼？他说不疼，看看还在不在。

到了夜里，她把他叫醒了。

小满睡在柴垛上——他跟他娘说屋里挤，要到柴垛上睡，他娘看了他一眼，给了他一床破棉絮——睡到半夜，只觉得胸口一凉，像揣着的一块冰忽然化开了，化成了水，从衣裳里一点一点往外渗。他一激灵坐了起来，那团银毛已经从他怀里钻了出来，蹲在柴垛顶上，对着月亮。

她的样子，比昨天更差了。银色的血是不渗了，可整个身子薄得像一层纸，月光能从她身上透将过去，照在柴草上，柴草上便有一小片亮。小满伸手去碰她，手指头穿进了那团银毛里，只觉得凉凉的，像把手伸进了一捧月光里。薄一分，又薄一分——她在谷里说的，原来是这个样子。

她道：「听着。本王要睡一阵子。」

「多久？」「不知道。伤太重，得闭关。」她看着他，「在本王醒过来之前，你得自己走。」

她从颈子底下一只旧得发黑的小布袋里——那布袋小满从没见过，也不知道她一直藏在哪里——一样一样往外吐东西。

头一样是一颗药丸，黑乎乎的，鸽子蛋那么大，一股说不出的怪味，像烂菜叶子泡了三天，又像他爹那双穿了一冬的靴子。她道：「洗髓丹。今夜就泡。疼，别喊。」

第二样是一卷竹简，绳子都快烂了，竹片发黄发黑，边上还有虫蛀的眼儿。她道：「《吐纳经》。最粗浅的入门功夫，仙界三岁的狐狸崽子都会。看不懂，也要背。」

然后她看着他，一个字一个字地说道：「**藏。**」

小满道：「藏什么？」

「藏本王，藏你自己。」她道，「在你打得过所有人之前，不许让任何人知道本王，不许让任何人知道你在修炼。能装傻就装傻，能示弱就示弱。——你那个吃饼的鬼，就很好。往后，你就是那个见了鬼吓得打摆子的傻孩子。」

「我娘也不能说？」

银月停了一停，道：「你娘，用不着你说。」

小满想起他娘理围脖的那只手，想起她那句「这条围脖，挺暖和的吧」，想起她蹲在木箱前，把那个布包拿起来又放回去的样子，便不再问了。

「那什么时候能不藏？」

「等你把欺负过你的人，一个一个，都踩在脚底下的时候。」

她的眼皮越来越沉，声音也越来越低：「还有……本王在找一个地方……一个名字……」她皱着眉，很用力地想，一双金色的眼睛眯成了两条缝，「……想不起来了。等你……听见了，本王会知道的……」

小满道：「什么地方？什么名字？你说个大概，我替你留心——」

她却已经不说了。她的身子在月光里一点一点地淡下去，淡得像一缕烟，像早上灶膛里最后那一缕青烟。

小满急了。他知道，这一回，她是真的要走了，不是睡着，不是昏过去，是要到一个他够不着的地方去，也不知道去多久。那个字，这时候再不说，便真的来不及了。他张开嘴。

「银月——」

她看着他。她已经淡得快看不见了，只剩一双金色的眼睛，还在月光里亮着，等着他往下说。

他张着嘴，那个字就在舌头尖上。可不知怎的，话一出口，却变成了：「……你还欠我一张饼呢。」

那双金色的眼睛，眨了一下。

她的身子化成了一缕银光。那缕光绕着他转了一圈，轻轻擦过他的脸，凉凉的，钻进了他怀里，钻进了吴婆婆给他的那块狐纹木牌。木牌上那只蜷着的小狐狸，九条尾巴里，有一条亮了，银的，一明，一暗，像在很慢、很慢地呼吸。

小满低头看着那块木牌，小声道：「……喂。」

木牌没有回答。

他又道：「你还欠我一张饼呢。」

木牌，暖了一下。

他在柴垛上坐了很久。月亮从柴垛这头挪到了那头。

他把木牌捧起来，凑到嘴边，很小很小声地说道：「银月。」

停了一停。

「谢谢。」

木牌凉凉的，没有暖。

那条银色的尾巴，照旧一明，一暗。它睡得太沉了，听不见。

小满捧着它，又想起她临走那句没说完的话，便一个字一个字地念给它听：「一个地方……一个名字……」

念到「一个名字」，木牌上那条尾巴忽然亮了一亮——只一下，比一明一暗都亮，像睡着的人在梦里听见有人叫了一声，眼皮动了一动——跟着又暗了下去，照旧一明，一暗。
story.en:
The next day, she didn't wake.

Every little while Xiaoman looked down at his chest. His mother asked if his chest hurt; he said no, he was just checking it was still there.

At night, she woke him.

Xiaoman was sleeping on the woodpile — he'd told his mother the house was crowded and he'd sleep out there; she'd given him a look and a ragged quilt — and in the middle of the night he felt his chest go cold, as if the lump of ice he carried had suddenly melted into water and was seeping out through his clothes bit by bit. He sat bolt upright; the bundle of silver fur had already crept out of his jacket and sat on top of the woodpile, facing the moon.

She looked worse than the day before. The silver blood had stopped seeping, but her whole body was as thin as paper; moonlight passed through her and lit a little patch of the kindling beneath. Xiaoman reached to touch her and his fingers went into the fur, cool, like putting his hand into a handful of moonlight. A little thinner, and a little thinner again — so this was what she had meant in the valley.

She said: "Listen. This king has to sleep a while."

"How long?" "Don't know. The wound's too deep; this king must go into seclusion." She looked at him. "Until this king wakes, you have to walk on your own."

From a little cloth pouch under her chin, old and blackened — Xiaoman had never seen it, and had no idea where she'd kept it — she brought things out, one by one.

The first was a pill, black, big as a pigeon's egg, with an indescribable stink, like rotten cabbage leaves soaked three days, or his father's boots after a winter's wear. She said: "Marrow-Washing Pill. Soak in it tonight. It hurts; don't cry out."

The second was a bamboo scroll, its cords nearly rotted through, the slips yellowed and black, worm holes along the edges. She said: "*The Classic of Breathing.* The simplest beginner's skill; every three-year-old fox cub in the Immortal Realm knows it. If you can't understand it, memorise it anyway."

Then she looked at him and said, word by word: "**Hide.**"

Xiaoman said, "Hide what?"

"Hide this king, hide yourself," she said. "Until you can beat everyone, no one may know about this king; no one may know you are cultivating. Play the fool where you can; play the weakling where you can. — That flatbread-eating ghost of yours is exactly right. From now on you are the silly boy who saw a ghost and shook with fright."

"Not even my mum?"

Yinyue paused. "Your mother — you won't need to tell."

Xiaoman remembered his mother's hand straightening the scarf, remembered her "nice and warm, is it", remembered her crouched at the chest, lifting out the cloth bundle and putting it back, and asked no more.

"Then when can I stop hiding?"

"When everyone who ever bullied you is under your feet, one by one."

Her eyelids grew heavier and heavier, her voice lower and lower: "And… this king is looking for a place… a name…" She frowned, thinking very hard, her golden eyes narrowed to slits. "…Can't remember. When you… hear it, this king will know…"

Xiaoman said, "What place? What name? Tell me roughly and I'll keep an ear out —"

But she'd stopped speaking. In the moonlight her body faded, bit by bit, thin as smoke, like the last wisp of blue smoke from the stove at dawn.

Xiaoman panicked. He knew that this time she was really going — not to sleep, not to faint, but to somewhere he couldn't reach, for who knew how long. That word — if he didn't say it now, it would truly be too late. He opened his mouth.

"Yinyue —"

She looked at him. She'd faded almost past seeing; only a pair of golden eyes still shone in the moonlight, waiting for him to go on.

His mouth open, the word right on the tip of his tongue. But somehow what came out was: "…You still owe me a flatbread."

The golden eyes blinked once.

Her body turned into a thread of silver light. The light circled him once, brushed his face, cool, slipped inside his jacket, into the fox-carved token Granny Wu had given him. Of the nine tails of the little curled fox on the token, one lit up — silver — bright, dim, as if breathing, very, very slowly.

Xiaoman looked down at the token and said softly: "…Hey."

The token didn't answer.

He said again: "You still owe me a flatbread."

The token warmed, once.

He sat on the woodpile a long time. The moon moved from one end of the woodpile to the other.

He lifted the token to his lips and said, very, very softly: "Yinyue."

A pause.

"Thank you."

The token was cool. It didn't warm.

The silver tail went on as before — bright, dim. She was sleeping too deep. She couldn't hear.

Holding it, Xiaoman remembered the unfinished words she'd left with, and read them to it one word at a time: "A place… a name…"

At "a name", the tail on the token suddenly flared — only once, brighter than any of its brightening, like a sleeper who hears someone call in a dream and whose eyelids stir — then dimmed again, and went on as before, bright, dim.
